summary.title: A quantitative measure for the organization of a system, Part 1: A simple case
summary.executive_summary: This paper proposes a universal quantitative measure for the organization of a system, grounded in the principle of least action from physics. The author argues that existing methods using information or entropy are insufficient and that the physical amount of action provides a more natural metric for system states. The core hypothesis is that the amount of organization is inversely proportional to the sum of actions of all elements in the system. The paper derives a mathematical expression for this organization measure and applies it to a simplified limiting case: a closed, two-dimensional system containing one free particle and one internal constraint. The model assumes no energy dissipation, constant mass and speed, and an isotropic medium. By applying Hamilton’s Principle, the author demonstrates that the actual trajectory of the element is the one with the least action. The study compares two states of the system where the constraint orientation changes the trajectory length. It is shown that the state with the shorter trajectory (lower action) possesses higher organization. Specifically, if one trajectory is twice as long as another, the corresponding state is calculated to be twice as well-organized. This result provides a method for comparing different levels of organization within the same system or between different systems. The paper concludes that this approach empowers natural and social sciences to quantify organization, facilitating the design of systems with higher perfection. Future parts of the series will extend the model to multiple elements and open systems, addressing time dependency and broader applicability.

A state with a shorter trajectory (lower action) is more organized.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This paper proposes a universal quantitative measure for the organization of a system, grounded in the principle of least action from physics. The author argues that existing methods using information or entropy are insufficient and that the physical amount of action provides a more natural metric for system states. The core hypothesis is that the amount of organization is inversely proportional to the sum of actions of all elements in the system. The paper derives a mathematical expression for this organization measure and applies it to a simplified limiting case: a closed, two-dimensional system containing one free particle and one internal constraint. The model assumes no energy dissipation, constant mass and speed, and an isotropic medium. By applying Hamilton’s Principle, the author demonstrates that the actual trajectory of the element is the one with the least action. The study compares two states of the system where the constraint orientation changes the trajectory length. It is shown that the state with the shorter trajectory (lower action) possesses higher organization. Specifically, if one trajectory is twice as long as another, the corresponding state is calculated to be twice as well-organized. This result provides a method for comparing different levels of organization within the same system or between different systems. The paper concludes that this approach empowers natural and social sciences to quantify organization, facilitating the design of systems with higher perfection. Future parts of the series will extend the model to multiple elements and open systems, addressing time dependency and broader applicability.

Research Context
Measuring system organization is critical for evaluating complex systems. Previous attempts used information and entropy concepts. The principle of least action has been applied to various systems. A universal criterion for organization is currently lacking.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to develop a model for calculating organization. The main idea is that organization is inversely proportional to action. This measure is considered natural due to the least action principle. The model will be applied to a simple limiting case.

Methodological Details
The model applies to a closed system in 2 dimensions. The system contains one element and one internal constraint. Elements are assumed to be free particles with zero potential energy. The Lagrangian is equal to the kinetic energy only. There is no energy dissipation in the system. Mass and speed of the element are assumed constant. Start and end points are fixed at opposite corners of a square. The constraint cannot completely block the element's path. The medium inside the system is isotropic.

Procedures And Architectures
Organization is defined as proportional to the inverse of sum of actions. For a single element, organization is the reciprocal of action. The action integral is derived using the Lagrangian. Time is substituted with trajectory length due to constant speed. The action integral is proportional to the trajectory length. Organization is inversely proportional to the trajectory length. Two states with different constraint orientations are compared. The state with shorter trajectory has higher organization.

Key Results
State 2 is better organized because l2 is less than l1. The difference in organization is derived as a function of lengths. If l1 is twice l2, state 2 is twice better organized. There is a 50% difference between the two organizations. The second state is quantitatively twice as well organized.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
The method uses the fundamental principle of least action. The model provides a quantitative measure for comparing organization. This facilitates the development of natural and social sciences. The result allows design of systems with highest perfection.

Contradictions And Limitations
The model is limited to closed, nondissipative systems. It applies only to one free particle and one constraint. Extensions to open systems and multiple elements are future work. The model assumes constant mass and speed.

Claims
Organization is inversely proportional to the physical amount of action in a system. The amount of organization is inversely proportional to action. Organization is set to the reciprocal of sum of actions. Previous methods used information or entropy. This allows quantification of organization in various sciences.
A state with a shorter trajectory (lower action) is more organized. State 2 is better organized because l2 is less. State 2 is twice better organized if l1 is 2*l2.  This provides a metric for comparing system states.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the boundaries and initial/final points. Figure 2 illustrates two states with different constraint orientations. Figure 2 shows the least action path in each state.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is a formula linking organization to inverse action. 2. The strongest evidence is the derivation showing shorter paths mean higher organization. 3. The future path involves extending the model to open systems and multiple elements.
